The realm was in an uproar, and no mistake.

Ever since the eighteenth of the eleventh month of Keiō 3, when at the Aburanokōji they cut down Itō Kashitarō, the arch-renegade who had broken the oath, Kondō had gone strange. He had lost his balance, no doubt.
The return of power to the throne.
Tokugawa Yoshinobu had petitioned the Court to give up the office of shogun.
What was to become of the realm?
"Kondō-san, a man keeps his calm at a time like this. He doesn't go milling about, pushed this way and that by the currents of the hour."

Toshizō all but shouted it, but Kondō's days were one continual whirl. Day after day he would take a body of corps men and go dashing about every quarter of Kyoto — to Nijō Castle to meet the shogunate's chief inspector Nagai Genba-no-kami; running to the Aizu headquarters at Kurodani to gather intelligence; and, to cap it all, going even to the Tosa residence — of the loyalist camp, though of a stripe somewhat sympathetic to the shogunate — to meet the councillor Gotō Shōjirō, and,
"Chōshū threw Kyoto into turmoil at the Hamaguri Gate affair, and it has shown no remorse. What is your view of that?"
and by picking such a hopelessly out-of-date quarrel he left Gotō at a loss for words. The truth was that the secret edict to overthrow the shogunate had already come down to Satsuma and Chōshū.
That day, Gotō Shōjirō rounded on the visiting Kondō with a roar.

"This is the very hour of the nation's peril. It is the time for Japan to raise up a unified state and stand against the foreign powers. After the return of power to the throne, the Imperial land must be of one heart and one effort, must set its own house in order, reform the abuses of three hundred years, and become a country that can speak to the foreigner squarely, face to face. This is no age for going on about Chōshū this and Chōshū that. While we squabble among ourselves over such things, the foreigner will take the country from us. From this day, every man of high purpose must set his very soul upon that. Well, Kondō-sensei?"
"Just so — every man of high purpose..."

was all he said, and then, "Isami, silent, departed without uttering a single word." This, to be sure, is from the record on Gotō's side, so Kondō is drawn there absurdly crestfallen; but by and large it must have been something of the sort.
Kondō had become too much the politician, so Toshizō reckoned.
(The state of affairs, this and that of it, is neither here nor there. Even should the tide run against us, to hold fidelity through to the end is what a man ought to be.)
In the record on Gotō's side, Kondō is said to have let slip: "I too wish I had been born into the Tosa han. Then, in an age like this, how much I might have done."

Plainly Kondō's convictions were wavering. Kondō Isami, who ought to have been a plain man of arms, and whose capacity was for just that, had now gained too much honor and station beyond his due, and had come, besides, to yearn after ideas and politics. There, so to speak, lay the comic unsteadiness of Kondō.
So Toshizō saw it.
It's a sorry business, he grumbled in private to Okita Sōji on his sickbed.

"The Shinsengumi has become the strongest band of fighting men left to the setting sun of the shogunal army. An organization of this kind is feared precisely when it is unmoving as a mountain, unhurried as a forest. And here is its own leader, dashing about among the great men of the shogunate and the han, gabbling away on the affairs of the hour — it can only earn him contempt."
"That... is so, isn't it."
Okita, as ever, looked up at Toshizō from his pillow with a noncommittal smile.
"Sōji, get well soon, now."
"Of course I will."
Okita smiled. That smile was, as it always was, so clear it frightened Toshizō.
"Sōji, you're a good fellow, you are."
"Don't, now."
Okita drew in his neck. Toshizō was somehow odd today.
"If I'm ever born again in the next life, I'd like to come back not with this hard, rank temper of mine, but as a man like you."
"Well — which of the two is the happier..."
Okita turned his eyes away from Toshizō, and,
"There's no knowing. Isn't it that a man has no choice but to live to the utmost by the temper he was born with?"
he said. It was an unusual thing for Okita to say. Perhaps he was beginning to give up on his own life.
Whether it was that state of mind that did it, his voice was clear.
Toshizō hurriedly changed the subject. For some reason, tears had been about to well up in him.
"I've been reading the books of war."
said Toshizō.

"When I read the books of war, a strange calm comes over me. I'm no great scholar of letters, but even so I was taught my way through the Analects, the Mencius, the Jūhasshiryaku, the Nihon Gaishi, and the like. Yet I've come to see that dabbling in such things only sets a man peering and second-guessing at his own convictions the way a bystander reads a game of go, and makes of him a man weak in the hips. Beside them, the books of war — the Sunzi, the Wuzi — those are good. What's written in them has one aim only: to smash the enemy. Sōji, look at this."
and he drew his sword with a flash.
The Izumi-no-kami Kanesada, two shaku eight sun. How many men it had already cut, he did not even remember the number.
"This is a sword."
he said. The heat in Toshizō's voice was not aimed at Okita as his listener. It was as though he were telling it to himself.
"Sōji, look here. This is a sword."
"It is a sword."
For want of anything else, he smiled.

"A sword is a thing the smith made for the one purpose of cutting men. The nature of a sword, its purpose, is plain and simple. Like the books of war, it holds one idea and no other: to break the enemy."
"Mm."

"But look at the beauty of that plainness. A sword — a sword is more beautiful than a beautiful woman. Gazing at a beautiful woman does not gird up the heart, but the beauty of a sword draws taut, gravely, the iron bowels of a man. A purpose should be simple. An idea should be simple. The Shinsengumi should live by fidelity alone."
(Ah — so that was what he'd been wanting to say.)
Okita went on smiling from his bed.
"Is it not so, Okita Sōji?"
"I think so too."
To this, at least, he nodded plainly.
"So you think so too, Sōji?"
"But, Hijikata-san,"
and Okita, after a short silence,
"what is to become of the Shinsengumi, from here on?"
"What is to become of it?"
Toshizō laughed dryly.
"What is to become of it — that's no thought for a man. That's a thing for women and children to say. For a man there's no thought but this: what is to be done."
"Then, what is to be done?"
"The Sunzi says:"
Toshizō clicked the long sword home, and,
"In plunder, swift as fire; in speed, swift as the wind; in movement, like the crash of thunder."

Toshizō meant, to the last, to fight for the shogunate. Whether the shogun returned the government to the throne or did whatever else, it was no concern of Hijikata Toshizō's. Toshizō had been born into an age of disorder.
In an age of disorder he would die.
(Is that not a man's dearest wish?)
"See here, Sōji — whatever becomes of the world, even if the whole shogunal army is beaten and surrenders and I'm the last man left, I'll do it."

And in fact, later on, when the shogunal armies everywhere had surrendered, or were on the point of it, Hijikata Toshizō remained as the last, the single, retainer of the shogun, and fought to the very end. But that we shall leave to the later unfolding of this tale.
"What I — Sōji —"
Toshizō went on speaking.

"Waver now, the way Kondō does, and — up to this very day, in the name of guarding the Shinsengumi as an order, we have cut down comrade after comrade: Serizawa Kamo, Yamanami Keisuke, Itō Kashitarō... it would come to asking what we cut them down for. When they in their turn submitted to my sentence, they died splendidly, like men. For me to falter here — what face could I show them below the ground?"
"A man's whole life,"
Toshizō said further,
"is a thing for the making of a beauty — one's own. That is what I believe."
"And I,"
said Okita brightly,
"so long as there is life in me, will follow you, Hijikata-san."
The situation shifted from day to day, and on the ninth of the twelfth month of Keiō 3, not two months after the return of power to the throne,
the Restoration of Imperial Rule
— the great proclamation of it came down.

The shogunal hatamoto stationed in Kyoto, the Aizu troops, the Kuwana troops, one and all refused to accept this "success of the Satsuma han's conspiracy," and a movement to open war within the capital swelled up among them.

"The shogun Yoshinobu is of the Mito line. Raised in a house that from the first set too much store by the Court, at this gravest crisis of the House he has gone weak in the knees before the Satsuma side's chant of loyalty, loyalty. The shogun has sold out the Tokugawa shogunate."
That the shogun had sold out the shogunate was a strange piece of logic, but there were those, even among the shogun's own vassals, who argued it at the top of their voices. All was chaos now.
Yoshinobu was a man of talent. In brains, and in an eye for the drift of the times, there was probably not one among all the lords of the realm to match him.
But against the Satsuma-Chōshū side, riding the current of the age, there was no withstanding move after move as they played them.
The atmosphere of the "times" in that day, Katsu Kaishū spoke of in later years.

"The momentum of an age is a truly fearful thing. Saigō [Takamori], Kido [Katsura Kogorō], Ōkubo [Toshimichi] — as individuals, none of them was any wonder to speak of (in another of his sayings Katsu praises Saigō to the skies as a man without peer in his generation). But because they came riding the momentum of this 'Imperial Restoration,' in the end even I was left with nothing to say. Yet as the tide of that momentum gradually stilled, the worth of the men returned to the ordinary, and those who had looked so very great turned out, unexpectedly, to be small."

While we are at it, let us borrow one more passage in his own words — how Katsu, who was also a critic of the first rank, saw the situation of the time. The quotation above, to be sure, was set down in shorthand just as Katsu spoke it; but what follows was jotted down by Katsu himself, in secret, as a private reflection at that very time, in Keiō 3, and for that reason the smell of the "times" is alive in it. Since it is in the literary language, however, the following is the author's free rendering.

"The Aizu han (the Shinsengumi included — the author) is stationed in the capital and charged with keeping order. Yet its thinking is narrow and hidebound, and it is earnest to no purpose. These men have no true notion of how the House of Tokugawa might be preserved. They take that very hidebound thinking to be their loyalty to the shogunate. In all likelihood, if things go on as they are, it is they who will ruin the nation [Japan]. In short, their vision is small, and they do not know where the urgent business of defending the country lies. (...) Will there not, at this pass, come forward a man who can calm the nation, and who with a broad design seen from a high vantage will not mistake the country's course? To think of it is to do nothing but heave a long sigh." (The author: it must be said that the one man among the shogun's vassals who saw the state of the country from a step higher than this loyalist-versus-shogunist quarrel was Katsu Kaishū alone. Or perhaps the shogun Yoshinobu did too. The rage of the Aizu samurai at Yoshinobu's "throwing the shogunate away" lay just in this difference of awareness.)

The moment he learned there were restive stirrings among the shogunal soldiers and the Aizu and Kuwana troops in Kyoto, Yoshinobu, to keep clear of it, promptly withdrew himself from Kyoto to Osaka Castle.
Until then,
"the greatest hero since Ieyasu"

he had been called; the Satsuma-Chōshū side had dreaded his ability, saying, "So long as there is Yoshinobu, the shogunate may yet endure." From this time began the transformation of Tokugawa Yoshinobu. Submission — that is, a thoroughgoing flight from the times — was the whole of the last shogun Yoshinobu's life from here on.

By the by: Yoshinobu thereafter went on living a life given wholly to withdrawal, moving from place to place, and how extreme his flight and submission were may be judged from this — that the next time he was granted an audience to pay his respects to the Emperor was, of all things, thirty years later, on the second day of the fifth month of the thirty-first year of Meiji. He "waited upon" his own former seat, the old Edo Castle, and was received in audience by the Emperor and Empress. The Emperor Meiji bestowed on him a pair of silver flower-vases, a length of red-and-white crêpe, and a single silver cup. This, and no more, was the return he received for handing back the government, after thirty years. From it one may reckon the tragic half-life of Yoshinobu.
With Yoshinobu's descent to Osaka, the shogunal army left Kyoto like an ebbing tide. The Aizu han, of course, along with it.
The Shinsengumi alone, however,
"for the guarding of Fushimi"
— under that name — was quartered at the Fushimi Magistrate's office.
In Kyoto the so-called shogunate-toppling forces, with Satsuma as their main strength, held the Emperor in their keeping.
The high command of the shogunate,
(war between the Satsuma-Chōshū in Kyoto and the shogunal army in Osaka might break out at any moment)
— for that reason, set the Shinsengumi at Fushimi, the very front line as seen from Osaka.
"There is no higher honor than this."
Even Kondō was glad, as well he might be. Should war come, it would be the Shinsengumi that first opened fire against the Satsuma-Chōshū.
"Toshi — you're pleased, aren't you?"
"Well enough."

Toshizō was busy. Breaking up the barracks at Kashō-chō, readying the baggage-train to load the arms and the rest, apportioning the war-chest from the corps' strongbox, and all the other command that went with the move — these were the vice-commander's work.
It came suddenly: they had to set out the very next day, the twelfth of the twelfth month.
"Toshi — it's our last night in Kyoto. Since we came up to the capital in Bunkyū 3, so many things have happened in this city —"
said Kondō, but Toshizō kept a hard face and said nothing. He was too busy with a press of chores to have leisure for such sentiment. No — that was probably not this man's true nature.

By nature he was, after all, the poet-master Hōgyoku (Toshizō's haiku pen-name). And more, Toshizō was a "haikai maker" who composed intensely sentimental verses. There must have been a rush of feeling in him.

"See here, Toshi. Harada Sanosuke and Nagakura Shinpachi have wives. And there must be no end of corps men with a woman they've pledged to. What do you say — send them all tonight to their several women, and make the muster for tomorrow's dawn?"
"I'm against it."
said Toshizō.
"Tomorrow is, you might say, a march to war. Let a man spend a whole night on parting from a woman and his fighting spirit goes dull. A single hour for parting is enough."
"You've no feeling in you."

Kondō was nettled, as well he might be. Kondō kept no fewer than three mistresses' houses. It was no wonder he was cross: to make the rounds of those three houses alone, a single night would not be enough.
(I too have my Oyuki.)
So Toshizō thought; but in this time of turmoil, neither Kondō nor he himself, the heart of the corps, could vanish from the men's sight for so much as an hour.
Desertion —
was what he feared.
Indeed, under conditions like these, take his eye off them carelessly and deserters would surely appear.
(A man who runs is no loss anyway; but let even one deserter appear and it touches the spirit of the whole. That is what I dread.)
So Toshizō thought.
"No — in any case —"
said Kondō.
"Tomorrow neither of us knows what will become of his life. To let them grieve their partings for one night — that is the way of a commander. Toshi, I'll gather the men now and give the order."
That night, Toshizō stayed behind.
Of the officers, the only ones who remained at the barracks were Toshizō the vice-commander and Okita Sōji on his sickbed.
"Tonight I'll nurse you."
Toshizō carried a writing-table into Okita's sickroom and wrote a letter.
"To Oyuki-san?"
Okita said from his sickbed.
"I've never met her, but do add a line for me — that Okita Sōji, too, prays for her good health."
"Mm."
Toshizō pressed a hand to his eyelids.
The tears were overflowing.
Were they tears of parting from Kyoto, or had his longing for Oyuki surged up in him, or had Okita Sōji's gentleness drawn out his sentiment despite himself?
Toshizō was weeping.
He fell forward onto the table.
Okita gazed steadily at the ceiling.
(Youth is over.)
Such was his thought. Kyoto would become, for each of the Shinsengumi men, the grave of their youth forever. In this city they were now about to bury all the memories of their passion.
Toshizō's sobbing would not stop.
